items.definition: The capacity to reproduce, which changes across the life span.
items.example: Fertility is not a number that stays the same for a whole life.

items.definition: The chance that conception happens in one cycle.
items.example: Fecundity is the word for the chance in a single cycle.

items.definition: An estimate of how many eggs remain in the ovaries, built from hormone measurements and sometimes a scan.
items.example: The ovarian reserve estimate describes a stock; it is not a statement about the odds.

items.definition: The point at which ovulation and menstruation stop.
items.example: Menopause is a biological event, not a date on a calendar.

items.definition: The transition before menopause, when the cycles often change.
items.example: She was in perimenopause, and her cycles had changed for a while.

items.definition: The age of the woman when her child is born, used as a medical label.
items.example: Maternal age is a label in the record, not a judgement about the mother.

items.definition: The age of the father when his child is born, used as a medical label.
items.example: Paternal age carries different facts from maternal age, and the change is slower.

items.definition: The felt push to act on reproduction because the window seems to be closing.
items.example: The reproductive urgency was real, and the deadline behind it was still unchecked.

items.definition: Pressure that comes from a deadline somebody else has set.
items.example: The timeline pressure came from the family, not from her body.

items.definition: An expectation that one generation passes to the next about when life should happen.
items.example: Generational pressure rarely sounds like a command; it sounds like an observation.

items.definition: The gap between the number of relationships you want and the number you actually have. It is a feeling, and it can occur in a crowded room.
items.example: A full calendar and a lonely February are not contradictions.

items.definition: Being cut off from other people without choosing it, and without the comfort that solitude brings.
items.example: Working from home every day turned into isolation by February.

items.definition: The state of being estranged from the people around you, from a group, or from your own life.
items.example: He worked in the same team for years and felt alienated from it.

items.definition: Being alone by choice, with no element of loss or distress. It is not the same as loneliness.
items.example: Two hours of solitude on Sunday is what makes the week work.

items.definition: The practice of choosing fewer people and refusing more, so that the chosen ones get more of you.
items.example: Her selectivity is not rudeness; it is a policy she applies to everybody.

items.definition: A level of quality or a rule of conduct.
The belief that a partner must match a complete specification exactly, with no deviation allowed.
items.example: Hyperfidelity is why the search stops before it has really begun.

items.definition: A link between two facts, so that one explains, limits or changes the other.
items.example: There is a connection between the load on the pump and the life of the seal.

items.definition: The state in which both sides give and both receive, checked by asking each side what the other gives.
items.example: There is no mutuality here: one of them does all the giving.

items.definition: A decision to keep something going at a cost to yourself, made again and again rather than once.
items.example: Commitment is not one decision; it is the tenth one as well as the first.

items.definition: The state of being able to make the decision of commitment now, with the time, the wish and a picture of the cost.
items.example: He has the wish and not the readiness, and he can tell the two apart.

items.definition: The willingness to be known by somebody new, which is wider than being selective or not.
items.example: Openness is not saying yes to everybody; it is letting one more person in.

items.definition: A strong dislike that turns a possible approach into an immediate withdrawal.
items.example: Her aversion to that kind of meeting turned into a refusal before she had read the message.

items.definition: The state in which the same goal pulls you towards it and away from it at the same time.
items.example: The approach-avoidance conflict is inside him, not in the other person.

items.definition: The question of when to marry, and the order of the events that answer it.
items.example: Marriage timing is two questions: when the marriage happens, and when the life does.

items.definition: The sequence of roles and stages people are expected to move through, in the usual order.
items.example: A life course puts study and work before children for most people, and in a different order for others.

items.definition: The age or stage at which a milestone is expected in a given community.
items.example: The normative timing is what people assume when they do not ask.

items.definition: The pattern in which the further a person goes in schooling, the later the marriage tends to arrive.
items.example: The education gradient is a pattern in a group, not a cause that works on one person.

items.definition: Living together as a couple without being married.
items.example: Cohabitation moved their date, because the shared life came before the legal form.

items.definition: The state of a group in which marriage is entered later than it used to be.
items.example: Deferred marriage is the name for a group-wide move to a later date.

items.definition: The total of the ages in a group divided by the number of people in it.
items.example: The mean age moved up, because a few people married much later than the rest.

items.definition: The age in the middle of a list: half the group is older and half is younger.
items.example: The median age stayed where the middle of the group was, even as the mean age rose.

items.definition: A planned event moved to a later date.
items.example: The postponement had a reason, and the reason was the contract.

items.definition: The state of being ready for a relationship, in time, money and emotional terms.
items.example: Readiness was not there yet, and she said so plainly.

items.definition: The money part of readiness: a steady income, some savings and a housing situation that holds.
items.example: Financial readiness is the money part of readiness; the rest is not a number.

items.definition: How far ahead the decision can see, which decides how urgent it feels.
items.example: Our decision horizons are different lengths, and that is the disagreement.

items.definition: The timing of the people around you, used as a reference point for your own.
items.example: Peer timing says everybody my age is married; peer timing is not a measurement of me.

items.definition: The pressure a family puts on the timing of its members.
items.example: Family pressure asks about grandchildren at the table, and the answer is a plan.

items.definition: The three-letter code that names a currency in the standard ISO 4217, used by banks, customs offices and computer systems.
items.example: Write USD on the invoice, not the word dollar, so the system reads it.

items.definition: The money the law accepts as the final payment of a debt, so that no one can refuse it as the wrong money.
items.example: The landlord must take legal tender for the rent, even when he prefers a transfer.
